notes.title: Two colours in one title
notes.body: Dark green letter faces sit beside olive offsets. The effect gives depth without turning the words into literal objects in a scene.

notes.title: A name given room

studyData.intro: Large green words and a red name make typography the entire landscape. Follow the details to compare what is visible, what can be interpreted and what the edition record establishes.

regions.label: Two large green words
regions.summary: BUMI and MANUSIA form two tightly stacked lines.
regions.question: What can you learn from the title’s shape before knowing what its words mean?

sections.heading: Green title in the image
sections.body: BUMI and MANUSIA form two tightly stacked lines. Dark green strokes occupy much of the central area, with tall letters and broad feet. The words dominate without needing a separate illustration, while pale spaces remain visible inside and between them.

sections.heading: A title read as language and shape
sections.body: The title can function as both language and shape. Even before someone understands Indonesian, the stacked masses establish the centre of the cover. Reading the words adds another layer: Bumi Manusia is commonly rendered in English as This Earth of Mankind.

regions.label: Olive edges give the letters depth
regions.summary: Olive-coloured areas sit beside the dark green letter faces.
regions.question: Cover the olive areas mentally. What kind of depth disappears?

sections.heading: Olive offsets in the image
sections.body: Olive-coloured areas sit beside the dark green letter faces. They are especially noticeable along long strokes and around the broad bases. The second colour follows the title’s geometry instead of forming an unrelated picture behind it.

sections.heading: Flat colour suggests depth
sections.body: The offset makes the letters appear to have thickness or a shadow, although the cover remains a flat image. Because both colours are relatively muted, the effect adds structure without competing with the brighter red author block below.

regions.label: Broad feet anchor tall strokes
regions.summary: The large title letters end in wide horizontal feet and projecting terminals.
regions.question: Which letter gives you the clearest example of a broad foot supporting a tall stroke?

sections.heading: Letter serifs in the image
sections.body: The large title letters end in wide horizontal feet and projecting terminals. These small extensions repeat along the two lines, joining tall vertical movement to short horizontal movement. Their pale surrounding spaces are as important as their green surfaces.

sections.heading: Wide feet give the letters weight
sections.body: The repeated feet can make the title feel planted on the page. Compare that impression with the narrow upper parts of the letters. This is a description of visible forms, not an identification of a specific typeface or its historical lineage.

regions.label: A small word identifies the form
regions.summary: ROMAN appears near the upper-left corner in a small warm-coloured line.
regions.question: Would a reader who missed this small word still understand what kind of object was being offered?

sections.heading: Roman in the image
sections.body: ROMAN appears near the upper-left corner in a small warm-coloured line. It is far less prominent than the title but occupies an early place in the reading order. It labels the work as a novel rather than supplying another title.

sections.heading: A small label sets expectations
sections.body: The label gives a reader practical information before the large central words. Its modest scale lets it serve that purpose without competing for attention. Compare how much space a genre label receives here with the space given to the author’s name.

regions.label: A second heading names a connection
regions.summary: KARYA PULAU BURU stretches across the upper area in green.
regions.question: What does this line tell you directly, and what would require another source?

sections.heading: Buru wording in the image
sections.body: KARYA PULAU BURU stretches across the upper area in green. Its letters are smaller and less decorative than the central title. The phrase names work associated with Buru Island; it should not be mistaken for the name of the publisher.

sections.heading: A place name opens a historical question
sections.body: The wording adds context through a place name while leaving the title visually dominant. This cover alone cannot establish the circumstances in which the novel was composed. Distinguish what the phrase states from any historical knowledge a reader brings to it.

sections.heading: Why Buru matters
sections.body: Penguin’s reading guide identifies this novel as the first volume of the Buru Quartet and links its composition to Pramoedya’s imprisonment on Buru. That source adds historical context to the visible place name; it is a record for the work, not evidence about this cover’s unknown designer.

regions.label: A long name becomes a red block
regions.summary: PRAMOEDYA ANANTA TOER occupies two large red lines below the green title.
regions.question: If the author name were reduced by half, what would become the cover’s main balance point?

sections.heading: Red author name in the image
sections.body: PRAMOEDYA ANANTA TOER occupies two large red lines below the green title. The letters are close together and fill nearly the same width. Warm colour separates the name from the cooler title without removing it from the central vertical arrangement.

sections.heading: Title and author share the centre
sections.body: The two blocks give title and authorship comparable visual importance. A viewer may switch between reading a work and recognising a person. The cover’s hierarchy supports that possibility, but it does not show how familiar any particular audience was with the author.

regions.label: A small emblem closes the left edge
regions.summary: A small dark green square mark sits near the lower-left corner.
regions.question: How does the emblem’s light-inside-dark structure differ from the title’s dark-on-light letters?

sections.heading: Publisher emblem in the image
sections.body: A small dark green square mark sits near the lower-left corner. Pale shapes cut into its dark field, reversing the cover’s usual dark-on-light relationship. The mark is compact enough to be recognised as a unit before its internal forms are resolved.

sections.heading: An identity mark at a smaller scale
sections.body: The emblem provides a different scale of looking after the large title and name. Its enclosed pale shapes echo the title’s internal spaces, but the mark’s role is identification rather than another illustrated scene. Avoid guessing a symbolic meaning from the small reproduction.

regions.label: The publisher signs quietly
regions.summary: HASTA MITRA appears beside the small emblem, with a much smaller line beneath it.
regions.question: Which information belongs to the visible imprint, and which comes from the library record?

sections.heading: Hasta Mitra imprint in the image
sections.body: HASTA MITRA appears beside the small emblem, with a much smaller line beneath it. The imprint occupies only a modest strip near the bottom. It is separated from the author by a substantial area of pale paper.

sections.heading: The library records a third printing
sections.body: The Riau Islands library record identifies this copy as a 1980 third printing from Hasta Mitra in Jakarta. That record supports the publishing context and printing statement. It does not identify the designer of this particular cover, so the maker remains explicitly unknown here.

regions.label: The paper is not an empty colour
regions.summary: The pale field varies in warmth and texture, especially near the edges.
regions.question: Which marks would you hesitate to attribute to the original designer?

sections.heading: Paper surface in the image
sections.body: The pale field varies in warmth and texture, especially near the edges. Small mottled marks interrupt its surface. These variations belong to the reproduced copy as we see it; the image does not establish when they appeared or how the original paper looked.

sections.heading: A worn copy changes how colour feels
sections.body: Age and reproduction can change how a design is perceived. A cream field may feel warmer than an imagined clean white one, but that response should not be turned into a claim that the designer intentionally chose every stain or uneven patch.

regions.label: A pause before the title
regions.summary: A clear band of pale space separates the upper wording from the large green title.
regions.question: Which gap groups information, and which gap separates it?

sections.heading: Space above title in the image
sections.body: A clear band of pale space separates the upper wording from the large green title. Similar pauses occur before the author and imprint. These gaps organise the cover into readable blocks without the use of ruled lines or boxes.

sections.heading: Gaps group words and separate roles
sections.body: The pauses help words of different sizes coexist. Compare the narrow interval between the two title lines with the larger interval above them: one groups words together, while the other separates kinds of information. Spacing does some of the work that colour also performs.

connections.title: Two colours build one title
connections.label: Face / offset
connections.text: Green letter faces and olive offsets follow the same contours, making the flat title appear to have thickness.

connections.title: A title balanced by its author
connections.label: Title / name
connections.text: The green title and red author name form two broad stacked blocks; colour separates them while similar widths connect them.
